paras: The manhunt for Roderick Lowry took place in and around Jackson, Mississippi, in July 1888, after Lowry, a nephew of Governor Lowry, was accused of beating his wife at the house of Mayor William Henry. Mounted posses failed to find him, and a local paper reported that threats of lynching were voiced openly during the search. He was arrested a week later in New Orleans, returned to the Jackson jail and bound over for trial without any violence against him.

According to the New Mississippian, which drew on interviews with the mayor and the chief of police, Mrs. Lowry had been whipped by her husband in Canton and came to Jackson for protection. On the advice of a kinsman, Col. W. L. Hemmingway, she took refuge at the residence of Mayor Henry. She had been married scarcely four months.

On Monday, July 23, at about 1 p.m., Lowry obtained an interview with his wife at the mayor's house, and when she refused a reconciliation he choked and bit her and broke a stoneware pitcher and a medicine bottle over her head. Mayor Henry drew his pistol to shoot the fleeing husband, but Mrs. Henry caught his hand. Lowry ran half a mile to the Pearl River and, by one dispatch, reached the canebrakes within fifteen minutes.

The mayor and sheriff quickly organized mounted posses, reported in the wire dispatches as forty men, and volunteers joined them in searching the woods through the night. The New Mississippian wrote that the assault was the sole topic of discussion and that "threats of lynching, if caught, were freely and openly indulged." Parties went by rail to Brandon and Canton, and officers searched near Charlie Buck's place in Rankin county after a reported sighting, without result. By the end of the week a Memphis Appeal dispatch called his escape "entirely successful."

On July 31 the New Orleans chief of police telegraphed that Lowry had been arrested there, and Governor Lowry issued a requisition naming Deputy Sheriff L. F. Chiles to bring him back. A Jackson correspondent wrote that many regretted the capture because he would be bailed and might escape punishment. On the trip back Lowry told Chiles he knew of the bitter feeling against him and feared personal violence; Chiles answered that the feeling had subsided once it was known his wife was not fatally hurt. To avoid the crowds at the depot, the officers took him off the train early and brought him to the county jail by a little-used street.

At his preliminary trial on August 9, his wife testified against him, and two doctors said her injuries were slight. He was held for the circuit court in a $2,500 bond and a $500 peace bond, and was also bonded on an older charge of shooting at a railroad conductor. No report of the case's final outcome was found.

Wire dispatches from Jackson and New Orleans ran in Savannah, Yankton, Atlanta and Memphis under headlines such as "A Mississippi Brute" and "As Ferocious as a Tiger," and they described the posse without mentioning lynching talk. The Memphis Appeal followed the case closely, calling Lowry an "Incarnate Fiend" in one headline and reporting his "Mortal Fears of Mob Violence" in another. No paper criticized the lynching threats.

Within Mississippi the story became political. The New Mississippian, whose account the Brookhaven Leader, Chickasaw Messenger and Grenada Gazette reprinted on August 2, charged that state-house employees who served as correspondents had kept the story from the New Orleans, Memphis and Vicksburg dailies to protect the Governor. The same account ended by hoping that "outraged law and decency shall have been avenged" once the fugitive was caught. The Brookhaven Leader added an editorial listing Lowry's earlier indictments and mocking the Governor's "pardon mill."

Accounts of Mrs. Lowry's injuries differed: an early New Orleans dispatch said her life was despaired of, Jackson dispatches said she was improving, and doctors testifying at the preliminary trial called her injuries slight.

reader.title: Manhunt for Roderick Lowry
bases: Posses organized by the mayor and sheriff of Jackson hunted Roderick Lowry after he was accused of beating his wife, amid lynching talk reported only by the New Mississippian; no mob attempt on him was reported and he was later arrested and jailed (A1, A6, A11).

No one was killed: Lowry escaped the posses, was arrested in New Orleans and was returned to the Jackson jail and bound over by justices (A5, A11, A13). The only violence threatened by a group was lynching talk in Jackson reported by the New Mississippian (A6).

Several independent dispatches agree on the assault, the posse of forty and the failed search (A1, A2, A3, A6); the lynching threats rest on the New Mississippian account alone (A6, reprinted A9, A10), with the later Jackson dispatch reporting only 'bitter feeling' and Lowry's fear of violence (A11).
